title: Negative-weight paths: finite routes, edge budgets and cycle influence
attribution: Original graphs, questions, distractors, worked explanations and transfer prompts for RecallWeave. Algorithm background: MIT OpenCourseWare, 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms (Spring 2020), Erik Demaine, Jason Ku and Justin Solomon, Lecture 12: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/resources/mit6_006s20_lec12/. No reference exercise, figure or passage is copied. AI assistance was used in drafting and implementation.

items.prompt: The only edges are S → T (2), S → A (5), and A → T (−4). What is the shortest S-to-T route and its cost?
options: S → T, cost 2
S → A → T, cost 1
A → T alone, cost −4
No finite shortest route exists
items.explanation: Both S-to-T routes can be listed: the direct edge costs 2, while S → A → T costs 5 + (−4) = 1. This graph is acyclic, so repeated negative cycles cannot lower the cost further. A negative edge can coexist with a finite shortest route.
items.transfer: Change A → T to −2. Which of the two routes is now cheaper?

items.prompt: A graph has vertices S, A, T and only S → T (2), S → A (5), A → T (−4). Add 4 to every edge weight. What happens to the direct and two-edge S-to-T costs?
options: They become 6 and 5, preserving the ordering
They become 2 and 1, because a common shift cancels
They become 6 and 9, reversing the ordering
Both become 6
items.explanation: The direct edge changes from 2 to 6. The two-edge route changes from 5 + (−4) = 1 to 9 + 0 = 9. A per-edge shift adds a different total to routes with different edge counts; it is not a general way to remove negative weights while preserving shortest routes.
items.transfer: If two routes have exactly the same number of edges, how does a common per-edge shift change their cost difference?

items.prompt: A graph has vertices S, A, T and only S → T (2), S → A (5), A → T (−4). The S → A → T route has finite cost 1. Why does the existing Dijkstra explorer refuse this graph?
options: Every negative edge makes every target unreachable
Its settlement guarantee requires nonnegative weights, even though another method can solve this example
The route cost 1 cannot be represented as an integer
A negative edge proves a negative cycle exists
items.explanation: The existing explorer deliberately admits only nonnegative weights. The acyclic negative-edge example lies outside that method's stated guarantee, not outside the definition of a finite shortest route. This continuation uses Bellman–Ford rather than changing Dijkstra's admission rules.
items.transfer: Distinguish 'this algorithm does not admit the input' from 'this input has no finite optimum' using the example.

items.prompt: Round k of this synchronous trace permits at most k edges. With source S, what does round 0 contain?
options: Every vertex has distance 0
Only S has distance 0 and route [S]; all other entries are unreached
Only vertices joined to S by a negative edge are reached
Every entry is already classified as unbounded-below
items.explanation: A walk using zero edges can remain at S and has cost 0. It cannot reach a different vertex. The round's null entries mean no route within that edge budget; final unreachable or unbounded-below classifications are made separately.
items.transfer: For a one-vertex graph with a negative self-loop, compare round 0 with round 1.

items.prompt: For S → T (2), S → A (5), A → T (−4), what are T's distances in synchronous rounds 1 and 2?
options: 1 then 1, because every edge is scanned in round 1
2 then 1, because round 2 can use round 1's route to A
2 then 2, because the first route must remain final
Unreached then −4
items.explanation: Round 1 reads only round 0, where A is unreached. It can use the direct S → T edge but cannot chain the newly discovered S → A route within that same round. Round 2 reads A's previous value 5 and offers 5 − 4 = 1 to T. An in-place edge scan has different intermediate-round semantics.
items.transfer: Reverse the order of the three input edges. Which distance rows should remain unchanged? What can still differ when equal-cost routes exist?

items.prompt: For an n-vertex graph, why is n−1 the relevant edge bound for a vertex whose shortest-walk cost is finite?
options: Every directed walk has at most n−1 edges
All negative edges can be removed without changing costs
A finite optimum has a simple route; repeated nonnegative cycles can be removed without increasing cost
Every graph with a cycle has no finite routes
items.explanation: If a finite optimal walk repeats a vertex, its intervening cycle cannot have negative total cost: repeating that cycle would destroy finiteness. Removing a nonnegative cycle does not increase the cost. Repeating this yields an optimal simple route, which visits at most n vertices and uses at most n−1 edges.
items.transfer: Why does this argument not permit reporting the n−1-round estimate as a finite optimum for a vertex downstream of a reachable negative cycle?

items.prompt: The edges A → B (−3) and B → A (1) form a directed cycle. What happens when a source-reachable walk makes two additional circuits before continuing?
options: Its cost decreases by 4
Its cost decreases by 2
Its cost increases by 4
Its cost stays unchanged
items.explanation: One circuit costs −3 + 1 = −2. Two additional circuits change the cost by 2 × (−2) = −4. If the source can reach this cycle and the cycle can reach a target, there is no lowest finite source-to-target walk cost: another circuit always lowers it.
items.transfer: Keep A → B at −3. What B → A weight makes the cycle cost zero instead?

items.prompt: Use S → A (2), A → B (−3), B → A (1), B → T (4), S → U (7), X → Y (−2), Y → X (1), with no other edges. Which vertices are unbounded-below from S?
options: Every vertex, because the graph contains a negative cycle
A, B, and T only
A and B only; a target outside the cycle is always finite
X and Y only
items.explanation: S can reach the negative A-B-A cycle, which can reach A, B, and T. It cannot return to S or reach U. Thus S remains finite at 0 and U at 7. X and Y have their own negative cycle but are unreachable from S. Cycle influence follows directed reachability, not the mere presence of a cycle somewhere in the graph.
items.transfer: Add T → U with weight 0. How does U's classification change even though its direct edge from S still costs 7?

items.prompt: Use source S and exactly seven vertices S, A, B, T, U, X, Y. The only edges are S → A (2), A → B (−3), B → A (1), B → T (4), S → U (7), X → Y (−2), Y → X (1). T improves from 1 in round 6 to −1 in round 7 and has no outgoing edges. What does this establish?
options: T must itself lie on a negative cycle
The round 6 value was the final finite optimum
T is an improvement witness and is downstream of a reachable negative cycle; it need not lie on that cycle
The graph must contain an eighth vertex
items.explanation: A decrease between the n−1 and n edge budgets is an improvement witness. A finite optimum would already have a simple route within n−1 edges, so this decrease identifies unbounded influence. T is not on a cycle because it has no outgoing edges; here it is reached after the A-B-A cycle. Witness vertices and cycle vertices are different notions.
items.transfer: A vertex can be affected without improving in this exact final round. Why must the solver also follow outgoing paths from all witnesses?

items.prompt: The only edges are S → T (3), X → Y (−2), and Y → X (1). From source S, what should the final report say?
options: S and T are finite at 0 and 3; X and Y are unreachable
Every vertex is unbounded-below
T is unbounded-below, while X and Y are finite
The report must reject the graph because it contains any negative cycle
items.explanation: There is no directed route from S into the X-Y component. Its negative cycle cannot occur on an S-to-T walk or on any walk from S. S and T therefore retain their finite distances; X and Y are unreachable from this source.
items.transfer: Change the source to X. Which component becomes unbounded, and which vertices become unreachable?

items.prompt: Use source S and vertices S, A, B, T, U, X, Y. The only edges are S → A (2), A → B (−3), B → A (3), B → T (4), S → U (7), X → Y (−2), Y → X (1). What is T's final result from S?
options: Unbounded-below because the graph still has a negative edge
Finite at 3 via S → A → B → T
Finite at −1 because two circuits are mandatory
Unreachable because zero-cost cycles forbid traversal
items.explanation: The A-B-A cycle now costs −3 + 3 = 0. Extra circuits do not lower the total. The route S → A → B → T costs 2 − 3 + 4 = 3 and is finite. The disconnected negative X-Y cycle remains unreachable from S. Strict improvement, not merely repeated traversal or a negative individual edge, matters.
items.transfer: What result should an isolated source with a zero-weight self-loop receive?

items.prompt: Use source S and vertices S, A, B, T, U, X, Y. The only edges are S → A (2), A → B (−3), B → A (1), B → T (4), S → U (7), X → Y (−2), Y → X (1), and B → S (0). What should the final result for S contain?
options: Finite distance 0 because a source can never be affected
The last bounded-round number as its final optimum
Unbounded-below, with no finite distance or shortest route
Unreachable because it has an incoming edge
items.explanation: The source can enter a reachable negative cycle and now return to itself. For example S → A → B → S costs 2 − 3 + 0 = −1, so repeated circuits lower the S-to-S cost. The report must label S unbounded-below and withhold a finite optimum/route; a bounded-round estimate is only one walk's cost.
items.transfer: S can still reach U along the edge of weight 7. After adding the return edge, why does U also become unbounded-below?
